questions.problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x(1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}.
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{-t}+f(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find the function $f(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x=-2t.
$$

*You may also wish to make use of the following result (constants omitted):*

$$
\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t=(t-1){e}^{t}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x=-2t.
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t}={e}^{\int 1\,\text{d}t}={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x{e}^{t} & =-2t{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{t}) & =-2t{e}^{t} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x{e}^{t})\,\text{d}t & =-2\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ x{e}^{t} & =-2\int t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ x{e}^{t} & =-2(t-1){e}^{t}+C \\ x & =-2(t-1)+C{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t)=C{e}^{-t}+2-2t
$$

and finally, $f(t)=2-2t.$

questions.problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+3(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}).
$$

If ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ then the general solution can be expressed in parametric form $(x(t),y(t)),$ where

$$
y(t)=(\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-3t+C}{(t-1)^{2}})f(t)+g(t)
$$

and $C$ is an arbitrary constant. Find $f(t)+g(t).$

*Hint: Under the given transformation, we have*

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1}=\frac{3}{t(1-t)}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

We're told that, under the substitution ${y}^{′}(x)=t,$ our d’Alembert differential equation transforms to the first-order linear equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1}=\frac{3}{t(1-t)}.
$$

We'll solve this equation using the method of integrating factors. Since this equation is already of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

we compute our integrating factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int P(t)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2/(t-1)\,\text{d}t} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|t-1|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-1)^{2}} \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our differential equation by $I(t)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(t-1)^{2}\frac{2x}{t-1} & =(t-1)^{2}\frac{3}{t(1-t)} \\ (t-1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(t-1)x & =\frac{3(1-t)}{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting the left-hand side as an exact derivative, and integrating both sides of the equation with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x(t-1)^{2}) & =\frac{3(1-t)}{t} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x(t-1)^{2})\,\text{d}t & =\int \frac{3(1-t)}{t}\,\text{d}t \\ x(t-1)^{2} & =\int (\frac{3}{t}-3)\,\text{d}t \\ x(t-1)^{2} & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-3t+C \\ x & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-3t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
x(t)=\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-3t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}.
$$

To recover $y$, we substitute $x$ into

$$
y=x{t}^{2}+3t,
$$

which gives

$$
y(t)=(\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|t|-3t+C}{(t-1)^{2}}){t}^{2}+3t.
$$

Finally, we conclude that $f(t)={t}^{2},\,g(t)=3t,$ and

$$
f(t)+g(t)={t}^{2}+3t.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the d’Alembert differential equation, defined for $t>0:$

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}-{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}
$$

Using the substitution $t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ the equation can be transformed to a first-order linear equation of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t).
$$

Find the functions $P$ and $Q.$

$\,\,P(t)=$
{{field-1}}$,\,Q(t)=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

In our case, we wish to transform the equation

$$
y=x{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}-{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}
$$

into a first-order linear equation for $x=x(t).$ We proceed in three steps:

**Step 1**: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to $x.$

We have the substitution

$$
t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=x{t}^{2}-{t}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x{t}^{2}-{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x{t}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({t}^{2}) \\ t & ={t}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({t}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({t}^{2}) \\ t & ={t}^{2}+2xt\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}-2t\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate $\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t-{t}^{2} & =2xt\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}-2t\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ t(1-t) & =(2xt-2t)\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{t(1-t)}{2xt-2t} & =\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{t(1-t)}{2xt-2t}.
$$

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2xt-2t}{t(1-t)}.
$$

**Step 3**: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2xt-2t}{t(1-t)} \\ t(1-t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2xt-2t \\ t(1-t)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-2xt & =-2t \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{2xt}{t(1-t)} & =\frac{-2t}{t(1-t)} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\frac{2x}{1-t} & =\frac{-2}{1-t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2x}{t-1} & =\frac{2}{t-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(t)=\frac{2}{t-1},\,Q(t)=\frac{2}{t-1}.
$$

Consider the d’Alembert differential equation

$$
y=x\cdot \frac{1}{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Using the substitution $t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ the equation can be transformed to a first-order linear equation of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t).
$$

Find the functions $P$ and $Q.$

$\,\,P(t)=$
{{field-1}}$,\,Q(t)=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

In our case, we wish to transform the equation

$$
y=x\cdot \frac{1}{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

into a first-order linear equation for $x=x(t).$ We proceed in three steps:

**Step 1**: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to $x.$

We have the substitution

$$
t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=x\cdot \frac{1}{t}+t.
$$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\cdot \frac{1}{t}+t).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\cdot \frac{1}{t})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(t) \\ t & =\frac{1}{t}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{t})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(t) \\ t & =\frac{1}{t}-\frac{x}{{t}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate $\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t-\frac{1}{t} & =-\frac{x}{{t}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t} & =(\frac{{t}^{2}-x}{{t}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{t({t}^{2}-1)}{{t}^{2}-x} & =\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{t({t}^{2}-1)}{{t}^{2}-x}.
$$

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{{t}^{2}-x}{t({t}^{2}-1)}.
$$

**Step 3**: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{{t}^{2}-x}{t({t}^{2}-1)} \\ t({t}^{2}-1)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & ={t}^{2}-x \\ t({t}^{2}-1)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x & ={t}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{x}{t({t}^{2}-1)} & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{t({t}^{2}-1)} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{x}{t({t}^{2}-1)} & =\frac{t}{{t}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(t)=\frac{1}{t({t}^{2}-1)},\,Q(t)=\frac{t}{{t}^{2}-1}.
$$

$$
y=3xcos\,(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+7{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}.
$$

Using the substitution $t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ the equation can be transformed to a first-order linear equation of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t).
$$

Find the functions $P$ and $Q.$

$\,\,P(t)=$
{{field-1}}$,\,Q(t)=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

In our case, we wish to transform the equation

$$
y=3xcos\,(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+7{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}
$$

into a first-order linear equation for $x=x(t).$ We proceed in three steps:

**Step 1**: Substitute, and differentiate with respect to $x.$

We have the substitution

$$
t=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Substituting this into the equation gives

$$
y=3x\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+7{t}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+7{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum and product rules and using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7{t}^{2}) \\ t & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+3x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7{t}^{2}) \\ t & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+14t\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Isolate the derivative and take its reciprocal.

We isolate $\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & =-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}+14t\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & =(14t-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}{14t-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)} & =\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}t}{\text{d}x}=\frac{t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}{14t-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}.
$$

Therefore, by taking the reciprocal of each side, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{14t-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}.
$$

**Step 3**: Express the derivative as a first-order linear equation.

Finally, we write this in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+P(t)x=Q(t)
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{14t-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)} \\ (t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =14t-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ (t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =14t \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)} & =\frac{14t}{t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(t)=\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)},\,Q(t)=\frac{14t}{t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}.
$$
